content: Ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammatory condition that affects the colon, with an annual incidence of approximately 10 to 20 cases per 100,000 individuals. While most patients with ulcerative colitis can achieve remission through available treatments, there remains a subset of individuals who do not respond adequately to firstor second-line therapies. Additionally, a significant proportion of patients experience adverse effects from current treatment options, necessitating the exploration of alternative therapeutic strategies. Probiotics, which are live microbial supplements, have been proposed as a potential treatment due to their ability to improve intestinal microbial balance, enhance gut barrier function, and modulate local immune responses. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate the efficacy of probiotics in maintaining remission in patients with ulcerative colitis, as compared to placebo, no treatment, or other interventions. A secondary objective was to assess the occurrence of adverse events associated with probiotic use. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, was conducted on October 31, 2019. Additional efforts included contacting study authors and probiotic manufacturers for unpublished or ongoing trials, as well as reviewing references of relevant studies. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing probiotics to placebo or other interventions in both adults and children with ulcerative colitis were included, provided that maintenance therapy lasted at least three months and remission was confirmed by clinical, endoscopic, histological, or radiological criteria. Data extraction and risk of bias assessments were performed independently by two reviewers, and outcomes were analyzed using Review Manager 5. The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE methodology. The review included 12 studies involving 1,473 randomized participants, primarily adults, with study durations ranging from 12 to 52 weeks. The average age of participants ranged from 32 to 51 years, with an overall age range of 18 to 88 years. Seven studies investigated single bacterial strains, while five studies used mixed-strain probiotic preparations. Most studies were assessed as having a high risk of bias due to issues such as selective reporting, incomplete outcome data, and lack of blinding, resulting in low to very low certainty of evidence. When probiotics were compared to placebo, it was uncertain whether there was any difference in the risk of clinical relapse (risk ratio [RR] 0.87, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.63 to 1.18; 4 studies, 361 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, it was unclear whether probiotics improved the likelihood of maintaining clinical remission compared to placebo (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.37; 2 studies, 141 participants; very low-certainty evidence). When probiotics were compared to 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA), there appeared to be little or no difference in the risk of clinical relapse (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.22; 2 studies, 452 participants; low-certainty evidence) or in the maintenance of clinical remission (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.25; 1 study, 125 participants; low-certainty evidence). The combination of probiotics with 5-ASA, compared to 5-ASA alone, also showed uncertain effects on clinical relapse (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.87; 2 studies, 242 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and little or no difference in maintaining remission (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.24; 1 study, 122 participants; low-certainty evidence). Adverse events were infrequently reported. Most studies comparing probiotics to placebo did not report serious adverse events or withdrawals due to adverse events. In one trial comparing probiotics to 5-ASA, 11 out of 110 participants in the probiotic group and 11 out of 112 participants in the 5-ASA group withdrew due to adverse events (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.46 to 2.25; 222 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Discontinuation was primarily attributed to gastrointestinal symptoms. In one study comparing probiotics combined with 5-ASA to 5-ASA alone, no withdrawals due to adverse events were reported. However, two other studies reported two withdrawals in the probiotic group due to serious adverse events, including avascular necrosis of the bilateral femoral head and pulmonary thromboembolism (RR 5.29, 95% CI 0.26 to 107.63; 127 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Health-related quality of life and the need for additional therapy were infrequently reported across the included studies. In conclusion, the evidence regarding the effectiveness of probiotics for maintaining remission in ulcerative colitis remains unclear due to the low to very low certainty of evidence from poorly conducted studies with small sample sizes. Future research should focus on adequately powered trials with a minimum duration of 12 months, comparing probiotics to 5-ASA rather than placebo, to better reflect standard clinical care for patients with ulcerative colitis.
